title: Benchmarking Quantum Simulations of the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick Model Using Large Tensor Networks
authors: Maggie Bao, Rushil Dandamudi, Jerimiah Wright, Joan Étude Arrow, Henry Zou, Vardaan Sahgal, Brian J. McDermott
abstract: As quantum computing matures, it is critical to benchmark its real-world problem solving performance against competitive classical methods, such as tensor networks. In this work, we leverage the Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) algorithm to compute ground state energies of the Lipkin Meshkov Glick (LMG) model as a comparative benchmark against popular noisy intermediate-scale (NISQ) algorithms like the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) method. By running DMRG on the NERSC Perlmutter supercomputer, we provide one of the largest LMG ground state energy datasets in literature, containing accurate ground state energies for systems up to 1400 particles. We compare these results with VQE and SQD implementations on an IBM Eagle quantum computer for comparison. VQE achieved results within 1 percent error for 6 particles, while exceeding that threshold for all other values while SQD extended that range to 17 particles, suggesting that in a noisy intermediate scale quantum era, subspace-based approaches may strike the best balance between accuracy, circuit depth, and noise resilience.
summary: The paper benchmarks quantum simulation techniques (VQE, SQD) by calculating ground state energies for the LMG model, using DMRG as a high-fidelity classical reference. It demonstrates that while DMRG scales effectively to large systems, current NISQ methods face limitations in accuracy and resource scaling when compared directly.
main_problem: The core problem is benchmarking the real-world performance of quantum simulation algorithms (VQE, SQD) against established classical benchmarks as quantum computing matures.
main_result: The study demonstrates that while DMRG provides a highly accurate classical reference for large systems ($N \le 1550$), current NISQ approaches like VQE and SQD show varying levels of accuracy limited by circuit depth, noise, or computational resources.
method: The authors employ three distinct methods: the high-accuracy Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) for classical benchmarking; Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) using parameterized quantum circuits; and Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD).
model_or_system: The benchmark system is the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) model, characterized by a specific Hamiltonian involving Pauli operators. This model allows for testing across varying system sizes ($N$) and interaction strengths.
key_observables: Ground state energies of the LMG model, relative error compared to exact solutions, convergence rates, and computational runtime scaling with bond dimension ($\chi$).
important_parameters: System size up to $N=1550$ (DMRG); VQE is limited to the $W=0$ regime; SQD performance is constrained by available quantum shots and circuit depth.
main_assumptions: The comparison is framed within the context of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, necessitating application-centered benchmarks over pure hardware characterization. DMRG relies on MPS/MPO representations.
figures_summary: Figures summarize DMRG's stability and scaling with bond dimension; VQE convergence shows erratic behavior at larger N; SQD analysis details gate counts and circuit depth limitations for specific state preparations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the LMG model as a benchmark, details the classical (DMRG) and quantum (VQE/SQD) methodologies, presents large-scale energy datasets, and concludes with a comparative analysis of resource scaling versus achievable accuracy in the NISQ era.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant because it provides quantitative metrics for comparing the scalability and noise resilience of emerging quantum algorithms against mature classical tensor network methods when simulating complex many-body Hamiltonians.
